title: Second declension: λόγος and ἔργον

objectives.can: Parse and form second-declension masculine and neuter nouns.

explanation.summary: A declension is a pattern of endings. The second declension is the pattern of λόγος (masculine) and ἔργον (neuter): learn these two and you can read most of the nouns in the lists of the last lessons, such as θεός, κύριος, ἄνθρωπος and υἱός.

sections.heading: Stem and ending
body: A Greek noun is a stem plus an ending. The stem carries the meaning (λογ-); the ending carries the case and number (-ος, -ου, -ῳ, -ον …). To decline a noun is to give it with each ending in turn. Take the form from a dictionary: the headword is the nominative singular, and the article given with it shows the gender.

The second declension is the group of nouns whose stem ends in -ο-, though that vowel is not always easy to see because it joins with the ending. Most of these nouns are masculine (-ος) or neuter (-ον). A few in -ος are feminine, such as ἡ ὁδός ('the road'); the article shows it.

sections.heading: Masculine: λόγος
body: The pattern of the masculine is -ος, -ου, -ῳ, -ον in the singular and -οι, -ων, -οις, -ους in the plural. The generated tables of λόγος and ἔργον, below the text, are made from the forms found in the analysed texts of the library; a dash means that a form does not occur there, not that it cannot exist. The vocative (a fifth case, used in addressing someone) has its own lesson.

sections.heading: Neuter: ἔργον
body: The neuter differs from the masculine in three cells: nominative singular -ον (not -ος), nominative and accusative plural -α (not -οι, -ους). Everything else is the same. Remember that in every neuter the nominative and accusative are alike, in both numbers.

sections.heading: A neuter plural subject
body: A neuter plural subject often takes a singular verb in Greek. In John 3:20 the subject τὰ ἔργα ('the works') is plural, and its verb ἐλεγχθῇ is singular. This is an idiom of Greek, not a mistake, and it is common; do not count it as an error when you meet it.

sections.heading: How to parse
body: To parse a noun, give its headword, case, number and gender. For instance, τοῖς λόγοις is dative plural masculine of λόγος. Work in the same order each time: check the article, then the ending, then ask which headword it is. Many endings are shared by different cases of other declensions, so the article and the context decide whenever the ending is not enough.

misunderstandings: Not every noun ending in -ος is masculine. ἡ ὁδός is feminine and belongs to this declension; the article tells you. Nor does every word in -ον belong here: the masculine accusative of a noun also ends in -ον (λόγον), as do adjectives, so look at the article and the phrase.
The neuter plural -α is not a first-declension ending. τὰ ἔργα is neuter plural of ἔργον.
The accusative plural of the masculine ends in -ους (λόγους), the nominative plural in -οι (λόγοι). Do not mix -ους with the genitive -ου.
The headword is not always the form you meet. A dictionary gives the nominative singular; in the text you will find all the other forms.

deeper.heading: Accent moves, stem stays
body: The accent of a Greek noun tends to stay on the same syllable as it is declined, but the rules of accent move it, or change its mark, when the length of the ending requires it. Compare the accents in the generated tables: ἄνθρωπος and ἀνθρώπου, for instance, are accented differently. You do not need the rules at this stage; learn each form as it appears and let the tables show you where the accent falls.
